extracted.intended_audience: readers of Voyage of the Beagle; naturalists, geologists, and general educated readers interested in field observation and interpretation
extracted.subtask_description: Making and interpreting field observations in natural history and geology (voyage/expedition-style journal): collecting specimens, noting behaviours and distributions, and drawing causal/geological inferences from spatial and temporal patterns. Emphasis on careful observation, controlled comparisons, and cautious inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base taxonomic/ecological conclusions on consistent occurrences
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject Latreille's supposition that the gossamer owes its origin indifferently to the young of several genera of spiders, because "spiders of the same species, but of different sexes and ages, being found on several occasions at the distance of many leagues from the land, attached in vast numbers to the lines, renders it probable that the habit of sailing through the air is as characteristic of this tribe."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeated, consistent field observations across individuals, sexes, ages and locations to accept or reject hypotheses about origins or behaviours rather than accepting explanations that ignore recurring patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer depth/location from lack of disturbance (negative evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: On circular and oval patches of steady pale light "the ship, which drew thirteen feet of water, passed over, without disturbing these patches. Therefore we must suppose that some animals were congregated together at a greater depth than the bottom of the vessel."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat absence of disturbance by a passing vessel (or other perturbation) as legitimate evidence about the vertical distribution of organisms; include the vessel's draft/size as part of the inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform controlled, timely observations and use them to evaluate hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations made directly after taking up the water gave different results from Ehrenberg's statement that particles retain irritability; Darwin notes allowing a net to dry and then finding it still sparkled twelve hours later, arguing the particles could not have remained alive so long.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record the timing and handling of samples (e.g., drying, delay between capture and observation). Use such procedural details to test whether proposed biological explanations (e.g., living particles) are plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer mechanistic, gradual explanations unless evidence requires catastrophe
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of extinction: Darwin argues that geology and fossil evidence point to slow and gradual changes rather than a single great catastrophe and that rarity often precedes extinction, so we should not immediately invoke extraordinary agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting extinction or landscape change, give priority to explanations supported by cumulative, gradual processes and multiple lines of evidence; avoid attributing change to dramatic events without compelling evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for rarity trends preceding extinction in the fossil record
rubrics_metrics.description: "If then, as appears probable, species first become rare and then extinct... the evidence of rarity preceding extinction, is more striking in the successive tertiary strata... it has often been found that a shell very common in a tertiary stratum is now most rare, and has even long been thought extinct."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating extinction from fossils, examine abundance trends across strata; decreased abundance before disappearance supports gradual extinction hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlate similar geomorphic features across distances to infer large-scale, equable processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin notes that the step-like plains "stand at nearly corresponding heights at far distant points" and concludes the elevatory movement and sea-erosion were "equable over long lines of coast."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correspondence of landform levels across distant locations as evidence for region-wide, uniform geological processes rather than local anomalies; include measurements of heights and spatial comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer very long timescales from cumulative small processes
rubrics_metrics.description: From the great bed of well-rounded pebbles and the slow attrition and transport of fragments Darwin reasons on the "long, absolutely necessary, lapse of years."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When many small processes (transport, rounding, sediment accumulation) are required to produce observed features, treat long time intervals as the parsimonious implication and quantify where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute function from morphological details cautiously, using adaptive reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: On an anomalous crustacean limb: the penultimate joint ends in three bristle-like appendages with minute cups "which seem to act in the same manner as the suckers on the arms of the cuttle-fish... I suppose this beautiful and most anomalous structure is adapted to take hold of floating marine animals."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inferring function from structure, compare to analogous organs (e.g., suckers) and propose adaptive roles consistent with the organism's ecology; frame such functional inferences as hypotheses ('seem', 'I suppose') subject to further testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple observations and natural history context to evaluate competing explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarding sea phosphorescence Darwin compares Ehrenberg's microscopic description, his own net experiments, regional prevalence in warm seas, and temporal conditions (e.g., calm weather after swarming) to argue decomposition and agitation of organic particles as the cause rather than solely electrical atmospheric conditions or living particles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh diverse data types (microscopic observations, repeated sampling, geographic/temporal patterns, experimental manipulations) before preferring one causal hypothesis over others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge uncertainty and the limits of causal inference from field data
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin repeatedly admits ignorance of precise causes (e.g., what causes guanaco curiosity vs timidity; 'how and when it is hard to say' about checks on species increase) and cautions that we are 'profoundly ignorant' of conditions of existence for many animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state where evidence is insufficient to determine precise causal mechanisms; avoid overconfident claims and note alternative plausible explanations.
